summary: The Supreme Court upholds most of Quebec's Bill 21 and says the notwithstanding clause has few limits; Ottawa fast-tracks the Mackenzie Valley Highway.
body: The Supreme Court of Canada on Friday upheld almost all of Quebec's Bill 21, which bars many public employees in positions of authority, including teachers, police officers and government lawyers, from wearing religious symbols such as hijabs or turbans at work.[^1][^4] Quebec protected the law with the notwithstanding clause (section 33 of the Charter), which lets a legislature override some rights for five years at a time. Chief Justice Richard Wagner wrote that the clause has no limits beyond its own text, and that Quebec used it validly.[^2][^4] All seven judges struck down one part: a rule that members of the National Assembly must uncover their faces, which breaks the Charter's democratic rights, something the clause cannot override.[^1][^4]

The court split on a quieter but important point. Four of seven judges said courts can still formally declare that a law violates Charter rights even when the clause keeps it in force; three said they cannot. The court did not make such a declaration here.[^3] Two judges wrote that the law's burden falls "most heavily on Muslim women".[^2] Reaction divided along familiar lines: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called it "a win for provincial rights", while the National Council of Canadian Muslims called it a dark moment and vowed to keep fighting.[^4] Before the ruling, Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon had called the clause an essential democratic tool.[^5] My read: provinces now know the courts will not stop them using it, so the debate moves to voters.

In Yellowknife, Prime Minister Mark Carney listed the Mackenzie Valley Highway as a "project of national interest" under the Building Canada Act, the first in the North. The planned 800 km all-season road would link Wrigley to the Dempster Highway, give about 1,900 Sahtu residents year-round road access, and cut the drive from Yellowknife to Inuvik from about 38 to 23 hours.[^6] The federal budget sets aside $3.1 billion over five years.[^7] Conservative MP Bob Zimmer called it "another photo op", saying Northerners are still waiting for a road.[^7]
differences: Supporters, including Quebec's government and Alberta's premier, say elected legislatures should have the final say; critics, including the NCCM and the World Sikh Organization, say the ruling lets governments strip minorities of religious freedom.[^4][^5]

reads.summary: A clear legal breakdown of the Bill 21 ruling: how the judges split on the notwithstanding clause, and what courts can still say about laws it protects.
